utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to go in private session for a short moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to address the representative of the Registry at the place of the videolink. First of all, can we check whether you can hear me, whether you can see me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated] I can confirm that I can hear you quite well. Good morning, Your Honours. I can only confirm that everything is set here. I hope you hear me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your words because I had to change my plug in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated] Good morning to all the Judges and to everyone in the courtroom. Hopefully everything is fine now. We may proceed. Can we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Let's check again that all the judges do. Could you please repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- not completely yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I first be informed about who is in the room at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]... a technician here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we invite you to escort the witness into the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we do that, can I just bring one matter to the Chamber's attention while that is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This morning we asked Mr. Monkhouse if he would contact the Court officer down there to have the witness review his statement because we had not met with him prior to this. So I just wanted to tell the Chamber we attempted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber was informed about it, and I take it that you will -- give follow-up in the questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, I start addressing you as Witness 61 because the Chamber is not aware of any protective measures sought by you. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I haven't asked for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, before you give testimony, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that will you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I can see that the Registrar has now handed out you to the text of that solemn declaration. May I invite you to stand and to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukasinovic. Please be seated. Mr. Vukasinovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kehoe, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your name for the record and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: V-u-k-a-s-i-n-o-v-i-c; D-j-u-r-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, is your date of birth 4 July, 1948?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. In Benkovac, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, did you -- do you recall meeting with members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 3 April 2007?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I recall it. I don't recall the exact date, but it was about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Without knowing the exact date, do you recall signing a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I signed the statement that I handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis still has some technical problems, but it's the balance between the different sources of sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's permission, if we could pull up 65 ter 1D75 -- 1D75, yes. For the court officer in Belgrade, that would be tab O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, do you recognise the document before you as the statement that you signed on 3 April 2007?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: And the document that I see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, did you have a chance to review this statement prior to beginning your testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you like to make any changes or clarifications to that statement at this time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: There is nothing I would like to change, and I stand by this statement in full, the statement that I made to the investigator of the OTP. However, I do have some remarks in respect of the spelling. Some of the names have been misspelled. But that is it not really very relate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If at any point, Mr. Vukasinovic, you want to bring a misspelling or some misunderstanding to our attention, please feel free to do so. Does the statement before you, Mr. Vukasinovic, accurately reflect what you told the Office of the Prosecutor back on 3 April 2007?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Completely, in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is the information that you provided in that statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: They're completely true, as far as I could recall at the time, because from the events themselves to the time of my statement, some 12 years had elapsed, and to the best of my recollection, this is the full truth. And it's not only to the best of my recollection, but also on the basis of my personal experience and what I saw and heard myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, if I asked you questions regarding the same matters that are contained in your statement, if I asked those questions again in court would your answers the same here today in court as those you gave in your witness statement, back in April of 2007?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would, in essence, be identical. Perhaps there would be some minor discrepancies because of the time elapsed and the fact that we forget, but the essence remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we would offer into evidence 65 ter 1D75.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with regard to the summary itself, I haven't had the opportunity to meet with this witness. I haven't explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I explain to the witness. Mr. Vukasinovic, Mr. Kehoe will now read a short summary of the statement you gave in 2007, which has now been admitted into evidence. That is to inform the public about the substance of your testimony, so you don't have to respond to any questions. It's just that those who are watching these proceedings are aware of what approximately is found in your statement. So, therefore, if you would just listen for a while when Mr. Kehoe reads the summary. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Djuro Vukasinovic was the deputy chief of the public security station in Benkovac during Operation Storm. On the morning of 4 August 1995, Mr. Vukasinovic was the acting commander of the Benkovac police station. Concerning the shelling of Benkovac on the morning of 4 August 1995, Mr. Vukasinovic notes that artillery shells were falling on specific locations, identified in his statement, among them the Benkovac military barracks. Mr. Vukasinovic is also aware of the decision to evacuate the civilian population of Benkovac in an orderly and organised manner during the afternoon and evening of 4 August 1995. That would be the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. You may please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I'm going to ask you some clarification questions concerning your statement which has been received in evidence. And the first question I would like to ask you is directed to paragraph 4 of your statement in the last sentence where you note that you were acting commander of the police station in the absence of the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it that the witness has a hard copy in front of him. That's at least what I conclude from the body language. Mr. Vukasinovic, do you have a hard copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the submission was tab O that we gave to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with that sentence, Mr. Vukasinovic, who was the chief of the police for the Benkovac station at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of police, or, rather, it was the police -- the station of public security, as part of the Knin SUP was Zoran Lakic. Personally, I was never appointed in writing to be his deputy. However, because our entire complement of -- our entire police force was in the area of Bosansko Grahovo in the then Republika Srpska, I stayed behind with a number of senior, older policemen and civilians who were involved in general administrative matters. In view of the fact that I was an inspector, it was considered logical that I should be the leader at the time as a Deputy Chief, but I never - and I would like to reiterate this - I never received a written decision on my appointment as Deputy Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Understood, sir. Was Mr. -- was chief of police, Mr. Lakic, was he on -- up in the Dinara near Bosansko Grahovo with the rest of the police officers on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for reference, Mr. President, that's in paragraph 6 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, and we're moving ahead because the statement is in evidence, in paragraph 16 where you talk about later on, on the 4th of August, police officers from Benkovac who walked to Kistanje. Did these police officers, Mr. Vukasinovic, did they tell you why they left their positions on the Dinara and walked to Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: They said that there was general chaos there. They told me firmly, they confirmed this, that there was general chaos in the -- in the -- among the ranks of the army of the then Republic of Serbian Krajina and that they had to leave their positions around Bosansko Grahovo, so they walked from there to Kistanje, and that's over a distance of some 30 kilometres. And on my part, I sent from Benkovac some means of transport so that they could be taken from Kistanje to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, if I could just stay with your answer, which Mr. President is on line 10 -- excuse me, page 10, line 4. When you talk about "general chaos," could you explain this general chaos that you -- to which you were referring, regarding the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I did not say -- I did not use the term chaos. I said disarray. I cannot say anything more specifically because I was not there myself. And I was warned before my testimony that I should only speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the latter part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I cannot testify as to what thinking was among the leaders in the area of Grahovo because I was not there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just inquire whether there is still a portion missing and what portion exactly it is. I mean missing in translation. Because the witness, after you invited him to repeat -- after the interpreters told us that they had missed part of the answer, the witness then continued. Is there any portion missing? Otherwise, Mr. Kehoe, perhaps you read the whole of the answer and ask the witness whether that's the complete answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I would like to - pursuant to the President's instructions - just reread your answer back and see if this accurately reflects your testimony or if you would like to change your -- correct anything. I asked you on page 10, line 11, Mr. Vukasinovic, if I could just stay with your answer which, Mr. President, is on line 10, excuse me, page 10, line 4. "When you talk about general chaos, could you explain this general chaos that you -- to which you were referring, regarding the army of Republic of Serb Krajina?" "A. First of all, I did not say -- I did not use the term chaos. I said disarray. I cannot say anything more specific because I was not there myself. And I was warned before my testimony that I should only speak the truth." In the interlineation, the interpreter did not hear the latter part of the witnesses answer. And Mr. Vukasinovic you continue and say: "So I cannot testify as to what thinking was among the leaders in the area of Grahovo because I was not there myself." Now, Mr. Vukasinovic, other than the comment by the interpreter, is there anything in there that was either left out, incomplete, or you would want to correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: This is basically the essence of what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, in your conversations with the police officers that came back, did they describe to you this disarray, and, if so, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have that much time. We didn't have that much time to talk about it because they came late in the evening on that date, the 4th of August, and the people needed to rest, so I sent them to their respective homes. Some lived in the town itself, and most of them were residing in the neighbouring villages. I just wanted to send them home for them to rest and to take a bath and prepare for the next day. We did not talk in detail about the situation in Grahovo, and I could see that they, themselves, did not know much about it because they were - how shall I put it - secondary people in all these developments. They were just mere policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I would like to address several other issues in your statement. And the first one I would like to talk about is your description of artillery targets in the Benkovac area. Initially, I would just like to ask you: What was the distance from Benkovac to the confrontation line on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: There were several lines. The first, if we look from the direction of the east relative to Benkovac, was in the village of Priseg where there practically was just one path, one ditch, rather, dividing our positions and those of the Croatian army. Going from the east to the west, a second line of separation was in the village -- between the villages of Vrana and Miranje Donje and on westwards up to Zemunik Gornji. If you're asking me about the distance to the city of Benkovac, if I understood you properly, I can also tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The first line which I mentioned is about 9 or 10 kilometres from it. The second one about 7 kilometres. And the final one, some 18 kilometres, I believe. I might be wrong, by a kilometre or two, but that is of no consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your statement, sir, in paragraph 7 you mention, on the morning of the 4th going to see a battalion of the 92nd Brigade, and, again, in paragraph 17, you say you received information that the 3rd Brigade had been told to evacuate. What army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina units were on the front line in the Benkovac area at that time? And I'm talking about the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to repeat your last question? There was an interruption in the interpretation that I was receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was referring in paragraph 7 and 17 to your mention of at least two units from the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina. In paragraph 7 you mentioned the 2nd Battalion of the 92nd Brigade, and in paragraph 17 you mentioned the 3rd brigade. I take it that's the 3rd Infantry Brigade. My question for you Mr. Vukasinovic is at that time on the morning of the 4th of August, what ARSK units were on the front lines in the Benkovac area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: This is generally known, our two brigades, one had the numerical designation 92nd, and the other one 3rd. These are -- 3rd Brigade. The 3rd Brigade. These are mixed infantry brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, where the 7th Mixed Artillery Regiment was deployed?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Benkovac, there was no such unit. Maybe you are referring to the 7th Corps headquartered in Knin which covered the entire area, including our own area in Benkovac. So it was not a regiment but a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, was part of that corps, the artillery part of that corps, was that deployed in the Benkovac area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I said that our brigades were mixed units so that they did include some artillery weapons of smaller calibres and some tank pieces. So there was no need for any special unit from the 7th Knin Corps to arrive in our area. This is out of my recollection, these things that I'm saying, and I believe them to be true. And if I can add, the situation frequently changed; namely, I was not a member of those brigades. I was a part of the police force, and possibly there could have been some units from the Knin area, but I wasn't aware of it. I -- I don't know that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the 92nd Motorised Brigade and the 3rd Infantry Brigade, where were the command posts for those units?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The command post of the first one that you mentioned was in the village of Biljane Gorjne, that is the so-called forward command post. And the forward command post of the 2nd Brigade was in the village of Sopot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as for the artillery that was attached to the 92nd Motorised Brigade and the 3rd Infantry Brigade, where was that artillery deployed in the Benkovac area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise decided answer to that question, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn our attention to that part of your statement that discusses locations of artillery fire by the army -- the Croatian army on the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President and Mr. Vukasinovic, I will be talking about paragraphs 3, 5, 7, and 12, where the witness talks about these various locales.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in your first paragraph, paragraph 3, you mention that you observed artillery fire around the petrol station. How many petrol stations were there in Benkovac, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In Benkovac proper there was just one petrol station which was in the direction of Biograd, some 600 metres from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was this located at the cross-roads, 600 metres from the centre of town on the road towards Zadar, close to the railway?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, at the cross-roads from which one road loads to Zadar, another one to Biograd, and two towards the centre of the town. It is some 400 metres from the railway station in the direction of the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to bring up a map which is 1D72-2159. And I ask you -- it's a blank map of Benkovac, and I ask oral leave to add it to the 65 ter list. It's just a blank map that I have turned over previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your request to add the blank map to the 65 ter list is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. President, it would be 65 ter 1D2723.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I just would like to show you a map of Benkovac, and it should be tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the court officer, Mr. President, could give the witness a blue marker so we can just briefly go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be given a blue marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, taking a look at this, the map that's before you, could you circle the cross-roads for the petrol station and mark that with the letter A?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by the names of these streets, but this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand the procedure is for the court officer to hold it up so that Your Honours can see it at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the court officer hold up and have the camera zoom in on where the marking was made. Now let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's over to the left just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you apparently -- yes, it's the circle and the letter A which now appears at the south-western part of town, where we find cross-roads close to the railway line, which bends there, from south-west to -- in south-easterly direction, or the other way around. Just whatever way you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually have two more. Would you like me to have them marked and then show them in toto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you first ask the witness to mark and then we'll have a further look to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now likewise, Mr. Vukasinovic, in paragraph 3 you also mention the firemen's hall. And before we ask you to mark that, Mr. Vukasinovic, were -- were there Territorial Defence offices located in the firemen's hall?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the vicinity of, but they were stationed at the firemen's hall in the offices on the first floor. They were civilian -- civilian defence. There was the fire-fighting society. And the information and alert centre to alert citizens in the event of an air-raid or generally speaking. There were no military units at the firemen's hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was the firemen's hall used as a locale where, when there was order to mobilize troops, those troops met? Did they meet at the firemen's hall?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need. If there was mobilisation, probably the men would immediately go upon receiving the call to their respective units. There was no need for any larger number of people to -- or men to assemble there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, on that map, Mr. Vukasinovic, could you circle the firemen's hall and put the letter B next to that location. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, likewise, Mr. Vukasinovic, in your statement, again at paragraph 3 you mention the Bagat factory? Now, do you recall a building called the cool storage that was located near the Bagat factory?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I remember. This is an industrial facility below the settlement itself to the east from the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: It was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the -- this part of the witness's answer. The last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said it was an industrial facility below the settlement itself, to the east from the railway station. And what did you say then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said east from the railway station, and then I said there was, in this industrial complex, a cool storage unit as part of the trading enterprise Agroprodukt. Further on towards the east was a building of the Kepol factory. And behind it another one of the Bagat factory. All these three buildings were some 300 metres distant from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Looking at the map in front of you, sir, can you circle the cool storage facility and the Bagat factory. Cool storage with the letter C; and the Bagat factory with the letter D.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not see all that well, or cannot see. But I suppose that this is it. And this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: So it will be a C -- a C to mark the cool storage. And the Bagat factory with a D?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: And this building in between is Kepol, the chemical industry facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the marked map would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1500, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1500 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move to paragraph 5 of your statement, Mr. Vukasinovic, and you talk about shelling in the area of Benkovacko Selo, and if we could bring up D1446, page 6. And for the purposes -- it's at tab 31, for the Registrar, map 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no objection to the Defence showing this particular map to the witness, because I believe this is the map produced by the Defence, you know, based on a couple of sources. And, you know, it would amount to leading perhaps the witness can be asked as to what he knows about the military positions present in that area. But showing this witness a map produced by the Defence with certain markings would amount to leading the witness. He would not be able to say anything about this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think if I might respond, Mr. President. I think that for clarity sake with regard to Benkovacko Selo, this area is depicted in the map. I don't think that is a subject of dispute. And I was going to ask him about a locale in that area that he mentions he sees a degree of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are quite a bit of markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. If I could take -- the page 6 that I put up, Mr. President, does not have any markings other than the grid references. If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see red dots with numbers on it. What is on my screen now, perhaps it is not the map that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then let's get this one from our screens, and if you would then -- I take it that there's a certain sequence. Would be an earlier one a later one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was the first one. We were looking at number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 6 of this tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of this sequence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that map has no targets on it. None of the red dots that we were talking about before. I mean, it does have Benkovacko Selo there. But none of the targets that we looked at before. It's just a map of roads and grid references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, you apparently have problems in finding a non-marked map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 6 in e-court which is 1D69-0149 has many red dots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite the Gotovina Defence team perhaps to show it to Mr. Registrar so that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one. Now, in order to avoid whatever confusion, is there consensus on what the identity of this map is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a -- the major arteries as you can see in the Benkovac area. The numbers reflected there are grid reference numbers, and they are not target numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that there is no objection against the roads being marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you have a map before you that depicts the general location of Benkovacko Selo. And how far was the -- was Benkovacko Selo area from the police station in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab number, Mr. Registrar in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is tab number 31, map 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be shown on the camera before it's shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that's the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems that this is the same one as we have on our screen now. Perhaps on the left top -- yes, I see the markings. Yes, please proceed. The map may be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, taking a look on this map, and you see depicted in there is the general area of Benkovacko Selo. And my question for you is: How far was Benkovacko Selo area from the police station?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Benkovacko Selo itself is physically connected to the town of Benkovac. If you're asking me about the area which came under shelling, the Ristici hamlet in the coniferous woods, that hamlet is some 700 metres distant as the crow flies from the police station in Benkovac, and it is to the north of the police station in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, was there was a cross-roads in the Benkovacko Selo area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: There is an asphalt road which leads to Obrovac near the pine woods which I referred to. There is a village road which turns left from the road leading to Obrovac. Then a bit farther on, there is another offshoot branching off from that road to another hamlet, that is from the road leading to Obrovac. There are no other road there, so there is not a classic cross-roads. There is one -- one road leading to the right, and a few hundred metres later on, there is another one which turns left from the road leading to Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with the use of a pen, Mr. Vukasinovic, could you circle that area that you were discussing of where these roads were and mark that with a letter A.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that this is a very small map. It will be very difficult to be precise in marking. But I believe that it is here. But I must add, there was another road which turned left, before the one which I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, if we can move -- you mentioned some shelling in the pine wood area of Ristici. And I ask you, are you aware of a warehouse called the Pladina [phoen] warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear that name. There was no warehouse in that area, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we look at an area just north of the area that you circled, was there a warehouse that the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina used as a logistics base.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Even before the war, during the war, and from what I hear, now as well, is an area where fairs are held. It's a fairground; in other words, that's where all kinds of different things are sold. And as part of that compound there is an building that was a catering establishment, a small cafe. There was a small shop, and there was also an area where lamb would be turned on the spit. Let me also say this. This area was used at one time for training of high school students in range shooting. But this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, could you, on the map before you, circle the area that is the forested area in Ristici, and circle that as B.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately around the 77 number here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at that location, sir, of B, and if you look to the right of the area that you circled as letter B, were you aware of any of those warehouses or buildings to the right being used as a logistics base for the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will offer this exhibit into evidence and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Map marked with A and B, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1051 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement you mention, Mr. Vukasinovic, of going up to see the 2nd Battalion of the 92nd Brigade and then going up around Obrovac. And in the third-to-last sentence you note: "At around 8.20 we reached the intersection where you can go either Benkovac, Obrovac, or Knin. The intersection was under severe attack and trees were on fire." Now, sir, was this in the intersection that was south of Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to say before that, that I did not go to Gornji Zemun to meet anyone, as it says here to meet the commander; rather, I took that road so that I could reach Obrovac because the Benkovac-Obrovac road via Karin, which would been the shorter way for Obrovac, was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- under fire. And in order to avoid this fire, I went via Smilcic and then returned via Pridraga to Karin. So to answer your question, yes, this is an intersection to the south of Obrovac. The northern road leads to Obrovac. The left road leads to Benkovac, and right road leads to Knin from the direction of Benkovac, viewed from that direction. This is the Krusevo village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was the area -- that was intersection that was under severe attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly as I've said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on line 25 -- page 25, line 6, it says the interpreter doesn't hear something. I'm not quite certain if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression that it was then nevertheless translated where the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They caught up. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, how far was this intersection from the centre of Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: From the centre of Obrovac, there are two roads -- well, actually there are two roads leading from there to the centre of Obrovac. The shorter way is about one and a half kilometres to the centre, and the farther, the roundabout way, is about 2 kilometres along. And let me just say this, this intersection is at a higher elevation than Obrovac. So in order to reach that intersection, you have to go up the so-called Burovacka -- or down the Burovacka slopes, so that viewed from this intersection, Obrovac is in a depression, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukasinovic. I would like to take us to another topic which is the evacuation from Benkovac on the 4th and later the 5th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we'll be referring to paragraphs 11, 14, 15, 17, and 18, where the witness discusses that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, turning our attention to the evacuation, were you aware of plans to evacuate Benkovac and other towns that were -- these plans being in existence before Operation Storm was launched?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. But I should have known it, had such plans existed. I should have known it, because I was, in a way, in charge of organizing traffic, traffic control, in situations such as these. I heard of this plan on that day, in the afternoon, I think it would have been around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., when I was informed by the then president of the municipality, Dr. Stevan Vuksa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I would like to show you a document. And this would be tab 10 in the documents. And this is D253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Kehoe. Could I ask a clarification of the last answer. You said you were informed by the then president of the municipality. Informed about what exactly?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I was informed that we should organise the displacement of the civilian, the so-called non-combatants, to the area of Srb and Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, do you know if the civil defence had any plans in place to evacuate the civilians from Benkovac, in the event of an outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I know of this. These were plans that were drawn up as part of the defence plan for the municipality. These plans were drafted, I believe, since 1974. Up until the war, they would be drafted by each organ separately, the civilian defence, the national defence. And these plans had to be drawn up for evacuation of the civilian population, not only in the event of an outbreak of hostilities but also of major natural disasters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vukasinovic, did you participate in these plans and this planning that the area had established prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: If I may correct you, I did participate in them, but before the war. Before 1991. I participated because I was supposed to take care of traffic control in the event of evacuations, because, at the time I was in charge of preparing these plans, the general defence plan -- national defence plans within the SUP. But this was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how about, sir, after the war, and during the war? Did you continue to participate in some capacity and, if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I did not; and after the war, of course, it goes without saying, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were aware, sir, of the evacuation that took place that you mentioned in your statement in the paragraphs that I've talked about, 11, 14, 17, and 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before we continue, could I have a further specification in terms of time of what is considered to be the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, when you were talking about the war, does that cover the whole of the period 1991 up to and including August 1995; or do you have a more limited concept of what you consider to be wartime -- the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The period of war is, in my view, the period between September 1991, when the then official army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was called Yugoslav People's Army took certain actions in the area of Benkovac municipality, up until the 5th of August, 1995, in the morning. For me, that is the war period, wartime period; at least as far as the Benkovac municipality is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vukasinovic, in paragraph 14 of your statement, you note that: "I returned to the municipal hall around 6.00 p.m., around ten people were at the meeting and assignments were given to each person to ensure that the evacuation was carried out in an orderly manner." Now, when the evacuation was carried out, Mr. Vukasinovic, did they do it pursuant to the plan that was in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, that was not the case, because panic set in as a result of the shelling, and as a result of misinformation, and also some news that caused unrest among the citizens. But already around 4.00, people began to take things in their own hands, and on their own initiative, used the vehicles they had at their disposal, cars, tractors, whatever they had. They started moving out from the town and pulling out in the direction of north, north north-east without any actual order being issued. So if there was plan, an evacuation plan, it was not actually necessary to implement it in practice because people had already started doing it on their own from the town and from the villages to the east, the south-east, and the south, and the south-west, and west of the town, as well as from Karin Gornji which is to the north of the town. In other words, let me wrap up. There was no need to implement any organised plan, if it existed, because panic had set in, and people started fleeing on their own initiative. On our part, we organised transportation by buses from the bus station, and we used the buses that we had at our disposal at the time. And also we used some trucks, some commercial trucks, owned by companies in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, in paragraph 16, the first two sentences it notes: "All the people in Benkovac were already panicked, so there was no need to appoint anyone to go around and tell them that they were to evacuate. The organisation of the evacuation was communicated to everyone by word of mouth. After this meeting at 6.00 p.m., the organised evacuation started. However, even before, people had been leaving on tractors and other vehicles they could obtain." Are those sentences that I read for you, are they accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I reiterated in my testimony, but I corrected myself a bit in the sense that I said that there was no need to implement any kind of organised plan because panic had set in and people started fleeing of their own -- on their own. And what I said, that there was information being circulated around orally, that's true. There was an order to implement an evacuation and to leave the territory -- for the civilian population to leave the territory of Benkovac and from the area of Srb in Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, when you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just to correct a -- there's a correction. It should read paragraph 15 and not 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. It should read 16. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, when you said that after this meeting at 6.00 p.m., the organised evacuation started, what organised evacuation started after the meeting that you talked about in paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I have just tried to explain this a moment ago. I said that it was not organised evacuation, because there was no need for that because people in panic had already begun to leave the area, this area of Benkovac municipality, using their own private vehicles. And I also said that we, if we can use the term, organised evacuation, for that purpose, we provided buses and some trucks that we took from these companies. So, as far as I'm concerned that was the only thing that was organised in this entire -- in this entire project of leaving this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also note in -- in your testimony at page 30, line 13, you say that: "... there was an information being circulated around orally, that's true. There was an order to implement an evacuation and to leave the territory -- for the civilian population to leave the territory of Benkovac and from the area of Srb in Lika." Who gave this order to implement the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I was relayed this order by Mr. Vuksa Stevan, by telephone. He was the president of the municipality. And he said that he had received an order to evacuate the non-combatants, the non-combatant civilian population. I don't know whom he had been ordered by; probably someone from higher level in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what time did you get this order, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I left around - I can't exactly say what time it was - but I think it was probably around 5.30 or 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, prior to coming here, have you spoken to anyone about your testimony in this case, within the last month?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I discussed it with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Savo Strbac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I apologise, I omitted him. I also consulted with him because we are on friendly terms, and he is involved in matters that relate to these trials here. So I just wanted to hear his personal opinion as to what my position should be and whether I had to exactly agree to testify on behalf of the Defence; that was the basic thing I wanted to learn from him, and he said that, yes, I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just reading what you said here concerning Mr. Strbac page 32, line 4, you said: "I just wanted to hear his personal opinion as to what my position should be ..." So you talk to Mr. Strbac about what you should say in this courtroom here today? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not accurate. And that is not what I said, if my testimony of a minute ago was correctly transcribed or interpreted. What I felt I could ask him was whether I needed to accept to testify on behalf of Defence, because I -- in view of the fact that I was a witness for the Prosecution, so that was a bit unusual, and I didn't know if there was a legal basis for this, that I could be called to testify here also by the Defence of Mr. Gotovina's, and in view of the fact that Savo Strbac is a lawyer, an attorney, he knew that this was legally possible, and he said that I had to accept to testify. And that was the only subject matter of the conversation between him and me, and this conversation was conducted over the phone. I called him at his home phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, did you discuss with Mr. Strbac the issue of whether there was an organised evacuation from Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when did you call Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean on this last occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were talking to him prior to coming here today, did you discuss the issue of the organised evacuation with him then, or did you -- as a matter of fact, did you discuss it with him at any time?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. There was no mention of evacuation in the conversations that I had with Mr. Strbac. I explained to you twice now already, what it was that I discussed with Mr. Strbac, and if you'd like me to repeat it, I can. You asked me when this was. I think this was last Tuesday. Because he was away on sick-leave or something. He had some surgical intervention, so I couldn't reach him before that day. I only was able to reach him on Tuesday, and this was my only contact with him since the moment that I received the information that I will be called to testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me address one last issue with you, and if I can refer to the brigades and military units that you had talked about. In paragraph 7 you talked about going and seeing a commander, or talking to a commander in the 92nd Brigade. And in paragraph 17 you note: "At 11.00 p.m. a soldier arrived at the police station and told me that the 3rd Brigade had been told to evacuate." Mr. Vukasinovic, during the course of the 4th, were you aware or did you know or learn that there was heavy fighting in the Benkovac area between the Croatian army and the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew in the area of Benkovac municipality, the only fighting was in the area of Zemunik Gornji, and I mentioned this in one of the paragraphs of my statement. I said that members of the Croatian army had taken up positions, had taken control, of some of those positions called oris.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Goles, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the fighting on the 4th of August, I had not heard of them. I did not hear of them. I mean, infantry fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in the fighting that you learned of in Zemunik, that you talk about or you refer to just in paragraph 7, that is where the 92nd Motorised Brigade was according to your testimony. In that particular area, did you learn that there was heavy fighting in that area between the HV and the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I have already explained this. I heard that there was fighting in the morning hours on the 4th of August and that the Croatian army had taken a position in the area of this village, the area that is called -- the position that is called Goles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now on this area that you are talking about, were you aware of the casualties that were suffered by the Croatian army in that area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely have no information of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that the line being held by the 92nd Brigade did not break at any time during the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. But let me reiterate, a portion of the area of Zemunik Gornji was taken by the Croatian army. This is the so-called Goles area. In other words, the Croatian army had broken through the Defence lines in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, staying with that, sir, you mention in paragraph 17 that the 3rd Brigade was evacuating on the night of the 4th. Were you aware that the 92nd Motorised Brigade didn't withdraw until late morning on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the 3rd Brigade, it was just by accident in talking with a soldier that I found out that they had already left their positions. I got that information as I indicated here about 2300 hours on the 4th of August. As for the 92nd Brigade, the situation was such that certain lines had been abandoned and some remained manned until the second day, i.e., 5th of August, in the morning, for reasons of lack of information. These were some forward positions towards the Croatian army, where, simply speaking, word had not reached the men there to the effect that they should withdraw. The men did not know that because of the absence of communications means. In one of the paragraphs I described how the communications system had been destroyed in the early morning hours on August the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. We will have a break, but before having the break, I'd like to hear from the first of the Cermak Defence and Markac Defence how much time they would need for either examination or cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have a couple of questions, Your Honour, maybe 15 to 20 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen to twenty minutes. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you tell us how much time you would need for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very short, Mr. President. Not more than 15 minutes; ten minutes at the most, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you will now be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vukasinovic. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, at the time prior to the commencement of the Operation Oluja, as you said, you informally discharge the function of the deputy commander of the police station, which, at the time was called the public security station in Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In Benkovac, in fact, I should like to correct you if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A slip of the tongue. I'm sorry, I meant Benkovac. Can you tell us, what the role was in the armed forces of the army of the -- in the armed forces of the Serbian Krajina of the police.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, we inherited this from the time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, when the police was one of the defence components of the Yugoslav People's Army. That remained that way, also at the time of the conflicts from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, which you gave to the ICTY investigators, and I refer to item 6, you stated that a large number of policemen were in fact engaged at Mount Dinara, in defensive roles after the fall of Bosansko Grahovo. Who was in command of those police units which were deployed on Mount Dinara at the defensive positions of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose the military command of the area. I, myself, was never there to be -- to have gained any experiences. But I assume that it was the military command of some of the units of the 7th Knin Corps. Members of the police were under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what types of weapons were issued to the policemen in discharging those duties?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly do. It was so-called personnel weaponry. They were rifles, whether automatic or semi-automatic, and pistols. The police units did not have any other armaments. Yes, there were the machine-guns which had the same power, firing power, as automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was this stored, the police armaments.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: It was within the police building in Benkovac. But there were few in the depot because they had been distributed to police members as personal weapons so they had them with them, both in periods of rest and in periods when they were in whatever way engaged at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. A different topic now. The question of the repeater at Celavac. In your statement, you say that Celavac is only -- was only some 3 kilometres distant, as the crow flies, from Obrovac, where you found yourself in the morning on the 4th of August and that when you entered the police station, you heard them say on the radio that NATO aircraft had attacked the repeater at Celavac. Could you clarify for us this segment of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I shall do my best. I arrived in Obrovac with a lad who was a car mechanic in your unit, because, the day before, a car had broken down, an official vehicle had broken down. When we arrived there, outside the police station in Obrovac, while actually entering the building, I heard via radio communications NATO aircraft are killing us off. So I asked the policemen on duty - it's not an officer as you state in your statement, as you write in the statement, but just a policeman - what was happening, and that is exactly what he said. We are being shelled by NATO aircraft at Celavac. Now why Celavac? Celavac is interesting for a number of reasons. First of all, because it had a complete communications equipment. Their system of the Republic of Serbian Krajina located there. So ordinary radio communications, television communication, special radio communications, special telephone communications, it was all there in that location. So I hope that I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your reply. And my last question, Mr. Vukasinovic, in your statement you refer to civilian defence also. Can you recall within which ministry was the civilian defence located?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian defence is a component part of the Ministry of Defence. It was so structured that the -- it was within the competent of the secretariat of national defence which was its name before the war. So this was a component part of the Secretariat for National Defence of every municipality and so was the case in Obrovac as well, and I can expand further if are you interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examined the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that you participated in drawing up evacuation plans which was part of the defence plan of the municipality. And those plans were in existence since 1974. And I'm referring to testimony at page 27, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D253, please, and it's in the -- it's in tab 7 of the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know the document -- do you have the Benkovac evacuation plan in front of you, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If it is not tab 7 perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Registrar, could you try tab 1. I'm sorry, it's at tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the same as O for the Defence, from what I remember. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can take a closer look at it, perhaps I will find that I'm familiar with it. Just give me a minute, please. I can tell you right away, no, I'm not familiar with this document. This was done by a service in charge of these matters and that was the civilian defence staff of the municipality, of which I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to bring only one page to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just turn to page 2, and you have to follow the page 2 because the chart has not been reproduced in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note the -- the evacuation routes that are noted on that page?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I can see them. It is -- they are drawn in very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that with the exception of the two locations at the upper right-hand side of that chart, that is Kistanje and Benkovacko Selo - I beg your pardon for my pronunciation - all the other destinations, or the upper most limits of this complicated evacuation plan, are within the Benkovac municipality? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But with your permission, I have to correct you. The "B Selo" in the right -- right upper corner refers to Biovicino Selo and not to Benkovacko Selo. That is the north of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that was my mispronunciation. And that place is within the Obrovac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: All these places are in Benkovac municipality, expect for Knin and Biovicino Selo which are in Knin municipality. All the other places drawn in this map, in this outline are in Benkovac municipality. And this other path is just a route indicator in case the need should arise to leave the municipality, at least I assume that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were involved in drafting -- or sorry, participated in drawing up the existing old evacuation plans. Isn't it correct that there was never a plan that was complicated to move the population beyond the borders of the Krajina under the existing old plans?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain, with your permission. All the plans, since they started to be drawn up, including the evacuation plan, were made to be implemented in the event of an attack by an external enemy. So in the period of the existence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, defence plans were drawn up to be implemented in the event of an outside aggression on the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This plan was of a quite different nature, and it only shows routes to leave places that might possibly come under an attack by a hostile force, so these are routes for relocation to the, so to say, rugged part of the Benkovac municipality, which is called Bukovica which has more natural shelters enabling the population to take shelter there. And the assumption was that an external enemy would not actually arrive with any major military forces in the area, in the event of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: And there, then I named the actual villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Vukasinovic. Now moving on I just want to take you to something you said in response to Mr. Kehoe, and that is at page -- page 30, line 13, for the record. Now -- if you could just bear with me for a minute, Mr. Vukasinovic. In response to Mr. Kehoe you said: "And what I said that there was information being circulated around orally, that's true. There was an order to implement an evacuation and to leave the territory for the civilian population, to leave the territory of Benkovac and from the area of Srb in Lika." This is referring to 4th August. Now, isn't it correct that -- the decision that was contemplated on the 4th was to evacuate the population up to Srb, up to Donji Lapac and Srb? I just want to see if there is a misunderstanding here in using the word "from," or did you mean to say "to Srb in Lika"? Do you understand my question, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand your question, and that is exactly what I said "to Srb," not "from Srb." So from the area of Benkovac, the thinking was that the civilian population should be relocated to Srb, because it was assumed that they not be in endangered there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And just one last question on that, Mr. Vukasinovic. From what you understood at the meeting in the municipal council building when the -- when you discussed with the others about organizing evacuation of the population, did you understand that evacuation to be of a permanent nature, where the population were to be moved outside the territory of the Krajina on a permanent basis; or did you understand it to be of a temporary nature, where they were to be moved out of harm's way, temporarily?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: When the action of the Croatian army started in the early morning hours of the 4th of August, the assumption was based on previous cases that the Croatian army would partially attack a part of our area. That is why the idea was that the non-combatants, the civilian population, should be moved away from that area for a temporary period until the action was over. However, what happened was that the Croatian army's action was comprehensive and final, and the population in question never returned but only went on farther afield. In implementing the decision that we carried out, we actually thought that this would be a short-lived exercise, that it would not involve the civilian population permanently leaving the municipality area. I hope that I have managed to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Mr. Vukasinovic, and I will be -- I'll finish off. Now in a response to a question posed by Mr. Kehoe, on the -- on the presence of -- as to who occupied or who was present at the fire brigade premises, you responded as follows. You said: "There were no military units." And this is at page 17, line number 10. Now were there any fighting forces at all at the firemen's hall, apart from organised units? I'm using the word "fighting forces," combat forces.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from members of the civilian defence, members of the fire brigade, and employees of the Secretariat of National Defence, and of the department -- or, rather, the early warning centre, there were no other units, especially not military units. The only facility in the area of the town of Benkovac, the town of Benkovac proper, was the army barracks. That was the only facility of a military significance, and there were none -- there was not -- no -- there were no others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you use the term "army barracks," you're referring to the Slobodan Macura Barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That was the only one in the municipality area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And today Mr. Kehoe discussed with you the cool storage and the two factories, Bagat and Kepol. Do you know what type of activity was being carried out in those three places, what was being manufactured? And I'm referring to the cool storage and the two factories, Bagat and Kepol.

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to some kind of a military activity, nothing -- no such production was going on, nor did we have any capacity or possibility for that. Bagat was the branch unit of the Bagat factory in Zadar, was not fitted out nor for the production of any equipment or armaments, and there was no need for that is correct because the Benkovac factory was outfitted for that and had the necessary personnel. Production went on only in the cool storage, but that was food processing or foodstuffs necessary for the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was going on at Kepol? What was being manufactured at the Kepol factory?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Kepol was also a branch firm of the Zadar and Zagreb Kepol. Before the war they produced chemical products, such as the tape, adhesive tapes, and that's it. If you mean -- if you mean potentially that they could produce some poisonous gases, that is absolutely out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you have referred to -- you list -- you note that you saw the petrol shed, the fire brigade, and the two factories being shelled. Isn't it correct that there were civilian structures in the direct vicinity of those places?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That part of town is to the south-east of the centre. It's part of a settlement, a neighbourhood of private homes, and in the immediate vicinity is also the railway station, and there were two residential buildings there with some 20 or so apartments, where families of people who worked for the railway were. So, this was the civilian population in their own private homes. That was what these facilities were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at paragraph 7 of your statement, and it was also dealt with earlier in direct examination, you testified that you saw the Benkovac-Obrovac-Knin intersection under severe artillery attack. Now, at the time you saw the intersection under attack, were there any ARSK members or units present at the intersection or in its direct vicinity?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, this was an intersection leading from Benkovac via Obrovac, to Knin. It is in the area of Krusevo village which belongs to Obrovac municipality, and there were no facilities there, other than a private home of the Tomljenovic brothers who also had a bakery there. In other words, a plant for the production of bread. So there were no other facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just have only two more questions, Mr. Vukasinovic. Now, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that when you went to the police station the shelling became more intense and that between 5.00 and 7.00 in the morning, approximately 100 shells would have landed. Now, do you know, or were you aware as to where those shells landed? Did they land on civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: DJURO VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That was my assessment, that that was the number of shells that landed there. As I described already, this started early in the morning and throughout -- and it went on throughout the day. As for the period when I was away, I don't know, but these are the figures that I mentioned. So the areas also that I mentioned are the areas of these three companies, the Bagat, the Kepol, and the cool storage, and then further on, towards the petrol station, the barracks, and the police station in Benkovac, and also in Benkovac village, the Ristic hamlet in the pine woods. I need not mention the names. As -- during the period when I was there, as far as I can recall, two shells landed, one of them, as I described in my statement to the OTP, one of them landed on a little hut at the football pitch. The hut is used for selling tickets, and the other one landed on the field itself where the -- in the area where the players who were not playing, who are sitting on the benches would be. In addition to this, there were also five or six shells that landed on the high school building which was in the immediate vicinity of the football pitch. And let me just say that the football field was next to the building -- next to the police station building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if perhaps the witness can take off his earphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness take off his earphones for a second. But let's first ask the witness whether he understands any English. Mr. Vukasinovic, do you understand English? Could you please take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, page 47, line 17, the witness prefaced that observation with a qualification, which I think is quite relevant.
